DECISION AND ORDER OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
LOCAL PANEL
On April 16, 2025, Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”) Donald Anderson issued a
Recommended Decision and Order (“RDO”) concluding that Respondent Chicago Transit Authority
(“CTA” or “Employer”) did not engage in unfair labor practices in violation of Section 10(a) of the
Illinois Public Labor Relations Act (“Act”), 5 ILCS 315/1 et seq., as alleged by Charging Party Erek
Slater. The Charging Party and Respondent each filed exceptions and responses to each other’s
exceptions. Upon review and consideration of the record, the RDO, and the parties’ respective
exceptions and responses, and briefs in support, we reject the parties’ exceptions and adopt the RDO
as discussed below.
Background and Summary of RDO
During the relevant time period, Charging Party was employed by Respondent as a bus
operator working out of Respondent’s North Park Garage and a member of the bargaining unit
represented by the Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 241 (“Union”). Charging Party was also a
part-time member of the Union’s Executive Board. The instant matter involves incidents that took
place during the period May 31 through June 5, 2020, that lead to Charging Party’s termination from
employment. As part of its response to the civil unrest in the aftermath of the death of George Floyd,
1

the City of Chicago requested assistance from Respondent to transport police officers. Respondent
agreed to transport police officers to and from a staging area but did not agree to transport detainees.
Charging Party alleges that Respondent unlawfully discharged him for his conduct on May
31 and June 3, 2020. He alleges that on May 31, 2020, he engaged in protected, concerted activity
when he went to an area outside Respondent’s North Park Garage that was not an area of CTA
operations to read part of a statement from the President of the Amalgamated Transit Union’s
International and discuss the implications of transporting police officers during civil unrest.
Charging Party further asserted that Jeffrey Smith, a CTA Senior Manager, approached Charging
Party and demanded that Charging Party stop the discussion, insulted Charging Party, threatened to
remove Charging Party from service, and called the police. Respondent contends that on May 31,
2020, Smith overheard Charging Party tell other bus operators to refuse to drive buses transporting
police officers. When Smith asked Charging Party to leave the property, Charging Party refused to
leave and continued to tell bus operators to refuse to operate the police shuttles.
On June 3, 2020, Charging Party arrived at the North Park Garage and informed Smith that
Charging Party was there to work the pick. Because Smith had been told by Keith Hill, President of
the Union, that Beseemah Dear-Townsend, Union steward for the North Park Garage, would be
working the pick, Smith called Hill who, according to Smith, confirmed that Dear-Townsend was
assigned to work the pick, not Charging Party. When Smith left his office to talk to Charging Party,
he saw that Charging Party was blocking the doorway between CTA Business Manager Lachowicz’s
office and the clerk’s office and asked him to move away from the doorway. Charging Party refused
to leave at first but later left the office area and went to the Union table in the pick area.
The ALJ found that Charging Party failed to establish that Respondent unlawfully discharged
him in violation of Section 10(a)(1) and (a)(2) of the Act. Applying the burden-shifting analysis set
forth by the Illinois Supreme Court in City of Burbank, the ALJ determined that Charging Party
2

failed to establish a prima facie case for retaliation under Section 10(a)(1) of the Act because
Charging Party’s conduct on May 31, 2020, i.e., promoting a partial strike or work stoppage, did not
constitute protected, concerted activity. Based on his credibility determinations, the ALJ found that
on May 31, 2020, Charging Party was advocating for a partial strike/work stoppage, which the ALJ
concluded was not concerted activity because Charging Party failed to establish that he was acting
on the authority of other employees. The ALJ also found this activity was not protected because it
solicited and induced other employees to refuse to work.
The ALJ next found that Charging Party’s reading of the statement from the President of
ATU’s International (“International”) on May 31, 2020, and Charging Party’s working of the pick
on June 3, 2020, constituted union activity but determined that Charging Party failed to establish that
Respondent bore any anti-union animus toward the Union or towards Charging Party’s union
activities.
Parties’ Exceptions and Respective Responses
Charging Party’s Exceptions
Charging Party filed 40 separate exceptions to the RDO. These exceptions generally fall into
two categories: (1) Exceptions to the ALJ’s credibility determinations, factual findings, and
evaluation of evidence (Exceptions 1-16 and 29-40); and (2) Exceptions to the ALJ’s findings related
to the applicable law and analysis, (Exceptions 17-28).
Exceptions to ALJ’s Credibility Determinations, Factual Findings, and
Evaluation of Evidence
Charging Party filed 28 exceptions challenging the ALJ’s findings of fact most, of which
were based on the ALJ’s credibility determinations. Four of those exceptions, Exceptions 14, 16, 37,
& 38, do not state the grounds in support of the exceptions and/or do not identify citations to the
records or cite legal authority as required by Section 1200.135(b)(2) of the Board’s Rules and
3

Regulations.1 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2). As such, we disregard these exceptions pursuant
to that rule.
We find the remainder of Charging Party’s exceptions to the ALJ’s credibility determinations
(Exceptions 1-13, 15, and 29-35) unpersuasive, and accept the ALJ’s determinations. The Board has
long held that credibility determinations are within the province of the administrative law judge who
had the opportunity to observe the witnesses’ testimony and demeanor. Chicago Transit Authority,
16 PERI ¶ 3021 (IL LLRB 2000). As such, we will not overturn an ALJ's credibility determination
unless they are clearly and demonstrably incorrect. County of Cook and Sheriff of Cook County
(Malone-Cole), 39 PERI ¶ 3 (IL LRB-LP 2022); Chicago Transit Authority, 16 PERI ¶ 3021 (IL
LLRB 2000); City of Chicago (Fire Department), 12 PERI ¶ 3022 (IL LLRB 1996).
Here, Charging Party has not demonstrated that the ALJ’s credibility determinations are
clearly incorrect, for the record lends support to the ALJ’s credibility determinations. As the ALJ
recognized, unfair labor practice matters often involve differing version of events. As reflected in
Charging Party's testimony and that of Smith, Hill, Dear-Townsend, and/or other witnesses, the
instant matter is no exception, thereby raising the question of which version of events was more
credible. The ALJ answered that question by finding Respondent’s version of events more credible.
He found Smith’s testimony credible despite Charging Party’s assertions to the contrary, basing his
credibility determinations on context, specific occurrences and items of testimony, demeanor, and
the fact that Smith was no longer employed by Respondent when he testified at the hearing. The
1 Section 1200.135(b)(2) states in relevant part:
Exceptions . . . shall specifically set forth the questions of procedure, fact, law or policy to which exception
is taken, shall identify that part of the Administrative Law Judge's recommended decision and order to which
objection is made, and shall state the grounds for the exceptions and shall include the citation of authorities
and citations to the record unless set forth in a supporting brief. . . . Any exception that fails to comply with
the foregoing requirements may be disregarded.
80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(b)(2) (emphasis added).
4

ALJ also found that Smith’s testimony was corroborated by the testimony of Dear-Townsend and
Hill, which the ALJ found, on whole, to be credible.
In contrast, the ALJ observed that Charging Party’s version of events relied primarily on his
own testimony which was not corroborated by the witnesses that Charging Party called to testify at
the hearing. The ALJ found that most of the witnesses that Charging Party called were not shown to
have been in a position to observe any of the conduct at issue sufficient to corroborate Charging
Party’s testimony. The ALJ further observed that the only one of Charging Party’s witnesses who
did observe at least part of the events in question was Juan Alvarado, but the ALJ found that
Alvarado’s testimony did not sufficiently corroborate Charging Party’s testimony.
Moreover, a review of the record, specifically the portions of the record identified in Charging
Party’s exceptions brief, fail to demonstrate that the ALJ's credibility determinations were clearly
incorrect. For example, Charging Party’s Exception 15 challenges the ALJ’s findings related to Juan
Alvarado’s testimony appearing on page 41 of the RDO. The ALJ stated that Alvarado “testified
that he saw Slater talking with 10-15 operators in the picnic area, that a manager (presumably Smith)
came out and told Slater that he was not supposed to be talking to the operators, that Slater and the
manager got into an argument, with flailing arms and screaming, that he heard that ‘they’ were trying
to organize a work stoppage or wildcat, and that he was not sure if ‘he did or didn’t.’” (RDO, p. 41).
Charging Party contends that the ALJ inaccurately stated Alvarado’s testimony. Charging Party
identifies the actual statement as “You know what, I heard that they were trying to say that he was
trying to do that, but I am not sure if he did or he didn’t.” (Tr. Vol.1, p. 309: 13-15). Charging Party
further contends that Alvarado testified that he did not observe any work stoppage organization,
citing Alvarado’s testimony at (Tr. Vo1. 1, p. 309:18-19). Charging Party claims that contrary to the
ALJ’s findings, these pages corroborate Charging Party’s testimony that he was not promoting a
work stoppage.
5

The portion of Alvarado’s testimony on which Charging Party relies, however, does not
demonstrate that the ALJ’s assessment of Alvarado’s testimony was incorrect. Although the ALJ
did not state word for word that portion of Alvarado’s testimony identified by Charging Party, the
rest of the ALJ’s statement, that Alvarado testified that he saw Charging Party and Smith arguing,
arms flailing, and that he was not sure whether Charging Party “did or didn’t” advocate for a work
stoppage, finds support in the preceding pages, (Tr. Vol. 1, pp. 306-08), and in the pages following
those identified by Charging Party (Tr. Vol. 1, pp. 312-14). We find the three remaining exceptions,
Exceptions 36, 39, and 40, likewise without merit.
Exceptions to ALJ’s Legal Analysis
We find Charging Party’s exceptions to the ALJ’s legal analysis, Exceptions 17-28,
unpersuasive. As stated above, the ALJ recommended dismissal based on finding the Respondent’s
version of the events of May 31, June1, and June 3, 2020, to be more credible than Charging Party’s
version, and the ALJ appropriately applied relevant Board precedent and caselaw to the facts that
conformed with the testimony he determined to be more credible. We find Charging Party’s
exceptions unpersuasive because they are rooted in the Charging Party’s version of events which the
ALJ did not find credible. For example, in Exception 27, Charging Party contends he was denied
due process because the ALJ failed to make any findings related to the allegation that the June 1,
2020 incident constituted a violation of Section 10(a)(1) of the Act, under an objective standard.
Charging Party contends that on June 1, 2020, he was talking to employees at lunch tables about
safety issues related to driving police shuttles when Smith came out of his office and ordered him to
stop, threatening to call the police if he did not stop. Charging Party contends that the ALJ failed to
address this allegation, ostensibly denying him due process.
This exception, however, is unavailing. First, as Respondent points out in its response,
Charging Party does not provide any legal authority that the failure to make such a finding denies a
6

party due process. The ALJ conducted 7 days of hearing, entertained several lengthy procedural
motions filed by Charging Party, and issued an RDO resolving the issue. It is unclear, and Charging
Party fails to explain, how Charging Party was denied due process. Although the ALJ did not
specifically address the June 1, 2020, incident under the Section 10(a)(1) objective standard, we find
that he did not do so because he credited Smith’s version of events.
The exceptions that contend that the ALJ erred in applying, failing to apply, or misapplying
specific cases are also unpersuasive. Charging Party’s contentions fail to undermine the ALJ’s
analyses, for the ALJ correctly applied the relevant Board cases and caselaw. Although NLRB cases
are persuasive authority, they are not controlling precedent for the Board and thus, the ALJ was not
obligated to apply the NLRB cases that Charging Party contends should have been considered in the
ALJ’s analysis. Moreover, in Exception 23, Charging Party contends that the ALJ incorrectly relied
on Electronic Data Systems, 331 NLRB 343 (2020), because the NLRB overruled that case in Ohio
Bell Telephone Co., 370 N.L.R.B. No. 29 (2020), a case that Charging Party claims is now
controlling. But the NLRB in Ohio Bell Telephone Co., did not overrule Electronic Data Systems.
Rather, the NLRB in Ohio Bell Telephone Co., found Electronic Data Systems distinguishable on
the facts.
Charging Party’s Request for Oral Argument
We deny Charging Party’s request for oral argument pursuant to Section 1200.135(c) of the
Board’s Rules and Regulations. 80 Ill. Adm. Code § 1200.135(c). Section 1200.135(c) of the
Board’s Rules and Regulations provides that “. . . [t]he Board shall grant or deny requests for oral
argument depending upon the significance, complexity and novelty of the issues.” Although length
and number of exceptions in this case may suggest otherwise, we find that the issues involved in this
case are neither significant, complex, nor novel.
7

Respondent’s Limited Exceptions
Respondent filed two exceptions related to the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party engaged in
union activity on May 31, 2025 and June 3, 2020. Respondent’s first exception disputes the ALJ’s
finding that Charging Party was engaged in union activity when he was, at least initially, at the garage
working the pick on that day but the record was not clear as to whether he was scheduled to work
that day. Respondent contends that both Smith and Hill testified that Charging Party was not assigned
to work the pick for the Union nor was scheduled to be at the garage for his regular work assignment,
and thus he was not engaging in legitimate union activity. Respondent’s contention does not
sufficiently undermine the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party was engaging in union activity on June
3, 2020. A review of the cited portions of Smith’s and Hill’s testimony supports the contention that
Charging Party was not assigned to work the pick for the Union or work for Respondent, but it is
undisputed that Charging Party was a member of the Executive Board and thus a union representative
and claimed to be there on Union business.
Respondent’s second exception also involves the ALJ’s finding regarding union activity and
is likewise unpersuasive. Respondent contends that the ALJ’s apparent finding that Charging Party
engaged in union activity on May 31, 2020, is incorrect. Respondent asserts that in analyzing the
Section 10(a)(2) claim, the ALJ assumed that Charging Party engaged in union activity by reading a
portion of the statement from the President of the Union’s International. Respondent contends this
is inconsistent with the ALJ’s finding that Charging Party’s activities on that day were not protected,
concerted activity. Respondent further asserts that such finding was based on the ALJ’s credibility
determination.
Respondent’s second exception fails to undermine the ALJ’s finding. The ALJ’s finding at
issue does not contradict his finding that Charging Party’s promotion of a partial strike on May 31,
2020, did not constitute protected, concerted activity. The allegations regarding the May 31, 2020,
8

incident involved two different activities: (1) the alleged reading of the statement from the President
of the International about safety issues surrounding driving police shuttles, and (2) the alleged
promotion of a partial strike/work stoppage. The ALJ appears to have focused on the partial strike
activity because that was the activity Respondent stated as the basis for Charging Party’s dismissal.
In sum, the ALJ’s findings, conclusions, and recommendations find support in the record and
applicable caselaw. Nothing in those exceptions undermines the ALJ’s findings and conclusions.
For the above reasons, we reject the parties’ exceptions as meritless and adopt the ALJ’s
recommendations for the reasons articulated in the RDO.
BY THE LOCAL PANEL OF THE ILLINOIS LABOR RELATIONS BOARD
